concepts.title: Adolescence: The Bridge Between Childhood and Adulthood
concepts.definition: Adolescence is the transitional stage between childhood and adulthood, marked by rapid physical growth, hormonal change and equally deep psychological and social change. It is the stage the learner currently occupies, which is why the course opens with understanding the self at this age.
concepts.key_idea: A bridge stage -- body racing, identity forming, relationships renegotiated all at once.
concepts.textbook_ref: kehe102.txt unit and chapter opening (stage of adolescence, physical and psychological change, understanding your own self)
question_patterns: why is adolescence called a transitional stage
in class 11 understanding oneself: what changes mark the onset of adolescence
why is adolescence described as a period of storm and stress
compare adolescence with childhood in terms of dependence
what is the significance of studying adolescence in this course
how do hormones influence adolescent behaviour

solution_steps.explain: Place adolescence between childhood and adulthood -- roughly the teen years -- as a bridge of transformation.
Growth spurt and secondary sex characteristics run alongside mood swings, self-consciousness and new social expectations.
The central task is identity: deciding who one is and will be, apart from parents.

concepts.title: Personal and Social Identity of the Self
concepts.definition: Understanding oneself means mapping the self along two axes: personal identity -- one's abilities, interests, values and aspirations -- and social identity, the roles one plays as daughter or son, friend, student and citizen. Healthy development weaves the two into a coherent self-concept and self-esteem.
concepts.key_idea: Two mirrors form the self -- the private one of abilities and values, the social one of roles and recognition.
concepts.textbook_ref: kehe102.txt identity sections (personal identity, social identity, self concept, self esteem, roles of an adolescent)
question_patterns: distinguish personal identity from social identity
in class 11 understanding oneself: what is self concept and how is it formed
what roles does an adolescent play in daily life
how does self esteem influence adolescent behaviour
explain how family and peers shape identity
describe yourself in terms of personal and social identity

solution_steps.explain: List your strengths, interests and values -- the private core of identity.
List the roles you occupy and the expectations each carries at home, school and among friends.
A stable self-concept aligns what you are with the roles you play, feeding realistic self-esteem.

concepts.title: Influences and Decision Making in Adolescence
concepts.definition: Adolescent choices are steered by family, peers, media and social norms -- sometimes in conflicting directions. The chapter equips learners to recognise these influences and to make reasoned decisions about studies, relationships, appearance and habits rather than drifting with pressure.
concepts.key_idea: Name the pressures before they name you -- decisions improve when influences are seen clearly.
concepts.textbook_ref: kehe102.txt influences sections (family peers media influence, decision making, peer pressure, responsible choices)
question_patterns: which influences shape an adolescent's decisions
in class 11 understanding oneself: what is peer pressure and how can it be handled
how does media influence adolescent self image
explain the steps of responsible decision making
give an example of a conflicting influence and your response
why do adolescents find decision making difficult

solution_steps.explain: Family expectations, peer approval, media images and social norms all pull at adolescent choices.
For any decision, ask whose voice is speaking and whether the choice serves your own goals and values.
Consider options, consequences and personal values before committing -- decision making as a skill.

worked_examples.question_pattern: A student is a class monitor, a tabla learner and the eldest child at home. Separate her personal identity from her social identities.

solution_template.explain: Monitor, music learner and eldest sibling are social identities, each carrying expectations.
Her patience with juniors or love of rhythm are personal traits that persist across roles.
Her self-concept weaves the traits into the roles -- self-esteem depends on how well the weave holds.

worked_examples.question_pattern: Friends tease a boy for not owning an expensive phone. Apply the chapter's approach to his decision.

solution_template.explain: This is peer pressure -- approval-seeking pulled against family resources.
Buying to please peers strains the family budget and feeds endless comparison.
A reasoned decision weighs need against cost and self-respect, not teasing.
